title: Was all of Africa colonised? Ethiopia and the battle of Adwa
subtitle: By 1914 almost all of Africa was under European control. Ethiopia's victory at the battle of Adwa, in 1896, is a main reason it was not.

parts.text: Many people learn that the whole continent fell under European rule. Almost all of it did, but not all.
By 1914 the whole continent, apart from Abyssinia (Ethiopia) and Liberia, came under European control.
The list is a simplification: other sources add small states, and we have not weighed them here.

parts.text: The Battle of Adwa was fought on 1 March 1896 near the town of Adwa in Ethiopia.
The Italian commander was General Oreste Baratieri.
Menelik won a decisive victory, securing Ethiopia's sovereignty.

parts.text: About 100,000, or at least 100,000 in another overview. The numbers differ between sources.

rows.ita: just under 45,000 troops available to Baratieri (likely the whole colonial force)

blocks.note: The sources disagree and we give each. Losses also differ: one overview says about 5,000 Italians were lost and about 7,000 Ethiopians died; a popular history says about 6,000 Italians dead and some 3,000 taken prisoner.

parts.text: Army sizes in the nineteenth century were estimated by the people fighting, and the Italian figure may count different things (those engaged, or the whole colony's force). Treat all of these as estimates.

The 1889 Treaty of Wuchale was written in two languages with different meaning. The Italian version of Article 17 said Ethiopia had to conduct its foreign affairs through Italy, making it a protectorate; the Amharic version said the emperor could use Italy's help if he wished.
Sven Rubenson's study speaks of a significant discrepancy between the Amharic and Italian versions of the article.
On 26 October 1896 Italy formally acknowledged Ethiopia's independence in the Treaty of Addis Ababa.
Adwa was a powerful motivation for Italy returning to Ethiopia in 1935.

blocks.prompt: About how many years passed between Adwa and the Italian return to Ethiopia in 1935?

blocks.q: Myth or fact: the Italian and Amharic versions of Article 17 of the Treaty of Wuchale said the same thing.
blocks.explain: The Italian version said Ethiopia had to conduct its foreign affairs through Italy, making it a protectorate; the Amharic version said the emperor could use Italy's help if he wished.

parts.text: Adwa became a symbol for Africans across the continent with which to identify.
It is celebrated as a symbol of national pride and resistance against colonialism.
A popular history calls it an international symbol of Pan-Africanism and Black pride.

gaps: The army sizes, losses and the dates of the Treaty of Addis Ababa rest on reference overviews and a popular history; Raymond Jonas, The Battle of Adwa (Harvard UP, 2011), is the book to read next.

Left out because no readable source outside Wikipedia supported them: the figures of 73,000 to over 100,000 Ethiopians against 14,500 to 17,800 Italian combat troops and 3,865 prisoners, and the claim that the victory was 'quickly' seen as a victory for Black people everywhere.
The statement that only Ethiopia and Liberia stayed independent rests on one encyclopedia article; other sources list further small states.
The Rubenson article was read only in abstract; its full text is paywalled.
No one from Ethiopia or Eritrea has read this page yet.

keyPoints.text: By 1914 the whole continent, apart from Abyssinia (Ethiopia) and Liberia, came under European control.
The Battle of Adwa was fought on 1 March 1896; Menelik won a decisive victory, securing Ethiopia's sovereignty.
The Italian and Amharic versions of Article 17 of the 1889 Treaty of Wuchale differed significantly.
Adwa became a symbol for Africans across the continent.
